question: Following recent changes to the Slovak Business Register, documents in its online collection of deeds are reportedly publicly accessible without the need for authentication. These documents may contain national identification numbers, identity document numbers, full residential addresses and handwritten signatures, creating a serious risk of identity theft and misuse of personal data.

The Slovak data protection authority has already raised concerns regarding this practice. It raises serious questions concerning the principles of data minimisation and data protection by design and by default under Articles 5 and 25 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), as well as Articles 7, 8 and 52 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. 1.
Does the Commission consider unrestricted online access to documents containing such personal data compatible with the GDPR and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union?

Is the Commission assessing the relevant Slovak legislation and practice, and is it prepared to take action, including infringement proceedings, should systemic noncompliance with EU law be established?

Has the development or modernisation of the Slovak Business Register received funding under the Recovery and Resilience Facility or other EU instruments and, if so, will the Commission verify whether EU data protection requirements and safeguards were respected?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.11.2026) While EU company law regulates the disclosure of certain information in relation to limited liability companies and commercial partnerships, it does not regulate the public access to deeds and to data contained in such documents in general.

With regard to limited liability companies and commercial partnerships, Articles 14 and 14a of Directive (EU) 2017/11321 require that a set of information about those entities, including information about legal representatives and partners, are publicly available in the national business registers.

However, Directive (EU) 2017/1132 does not harmonise the personal data categories to be made publicly available at national level. It is up to Member States to ensure compliance with the rules set by General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)2, as is affirmed by recitals 37 and 38 of Directive (EU) 2025/25.

Member States can provide for different disclosure requirements as regards personal data, provided these are necessary and proportionate to achieve an objective of public interest, such as the proper functioning of the internal market3.

Without prejudice to the competences of the Commission as guardian of the Treaties, Member States have a primary responsibility to monitor the application of the relevant legal provisions and to take the necessary steps for enforcement. Enforcement of the GDPR lies with the national data protection authorities and courts.
The Commission understands that the Slovak data protection authority is investigating this matter.
1 Directive (EU) 2017/1132 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 June 2017 relating to certain

aspects of company law (codification), OJ L 169, 30.6.2017, p. 46–126. 2 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation),OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1–88 https://eur-lex.europa.
eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng. 3 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 09 March, Manni, C-398/15, ECLI:EU:C:2017:197, see in particular paragraph 60.
